standardsFrameworkItems.description: Interpret and compute quotients of fractions, and solve word problems involving division of fractions by fractions, e.g., by using visual fraction models and equations to represent the problem. *For example, create a story context for $(\frac{2}{3}) \div (\frac{3}{4})$ and use a visual fraction model to show the quotient; use the relationship between multiplication and division to explain that $(\frac{2}{3}) \div (\frac{3}{4}) = \frac{8}{9}$ because $\frac{3}{4}$ of $\frac{8}{9}$ is $\frac{2}{3}$. (In general, $(\frac{a}{b}) \div (\frac{c}{d}) = \frac{ad}{bc}$.) How much chocolate will each person get if 3 people share $\frac{1}{2}$ lb of chocolate equally? How many $\frac{3}{4}$-cup servings are in $\frac{2}{3}$ of a cup of yogurt? How wide is a rectangular strip of land with length $\frac{3}{4}$ mi and area $\frac{1}{2}$ square mi?*

standardsFrameworkItemsbuildsTowards.description: Understand division as an unknown-factor problem. *For example, find $32 \div 8$ by finding the number that makes 32 when multiplied by 8.*
Apply and extend previous understandings of division to divide unit fractions by whole numbers and whole numbers by unit fractions.

buildsTowardsStandardsFrameworkItems.description: Solve real-world and mathematical problems by writing and solving equations of the form $x + p = q$ and $px = q$ for cases in which $p$, $q$ and $x$ are all nonnegative rational numbers.
Apply properties of operations as strategies to multiply and divide rational numbers.

Informally assess the degree of visual overlap of two numerical data distributions with similar variabilities, measuring the difference between the centers by expressing it as a multiple of a measure of variability. *For example, the mean height of players on the basketball team is 10 cm greater than the mean height of players on the soccer team, about twice the variability (mean absolute deviation) on either team; on a dot plot, the separation between the two distributions of heights is noticeable.*

strategiestargetsFactor.name: Math Centers

strategiestargetsFactor.name: Gestures

strategiestargetsFactor.name: Guided Practice

strategiestargetsFactor.name: Jigsaw

strategiestargetsFactor.name: Strengths-based Approach
strategiestargetsFactor.description: A strengths-based approach is one where educators intentionally identify, communicate, and harness students' assets, across many aspects of the whole child, in order to empower them to flourish.

strategiestargetsFactor.name: Translanguaging
strategiestargetsFactor.description: Translanguaging is a flexible classroom practice enabling students to listen, speak, read, and write across their multiple languages or dialects, even if the teacher does not have formal knowledge of these additional languages.

strategiestargetsFactor.name: Writing to Learn Math
strategiestargetsFactor.description: Writing that encourages students to articulate their understanding of math concepts or explain math ideas helps deepen students' mathematical understanding.

strategiestargetsFactor.name: Concrete-Representational-Abstract (CRA)
strategiestargetsFactor.description: CRA is a sequential instructional approach during which students move from working with concrete materials to creating representational drawings to using abstract symbols.

strategiestargetsFactor.name: Direct Instruction: Math Vocabulary
strategiestargetsFactor.description: Knowing the language of math is critical because students must use this language to understand math concepts and determine calculations needed.

strategiestargetsFactor.name: Direct Instruction: Patterning
strategiestargetsFactor.description: Thinking of and about patterns encourages learners to look for and understand the rules and relationships that are critical components of mathematical reasoning.

strategiestargetsFactor.name: Flexible Grouping
strategiestargetsFactor.description: Flexible grouping is a classroom practice that temporarily places students together in given groups to work together, with the purpose of achieving a given learning goal or activity.

strategiestargetsFactor.name: Foster Growth Mindset
strategiestargetsFactor.description: Teachers can help students understand that learning involves effort, mistakes, and reflection by teaching them about their malleable brain and modeling their own learning process.

strategiestargetsFactor.name: Math Games
strategiestargetsFactor.description: Math games allow students to practice many math skills in a fun, applied context.

strategiestargetsFactor.name: Multiple Methods of Assessment
strategiestargetsFactor.description: Using multiple methods of assessment can help educators gain a comprehensive understanding of learner progress across a wide range of skills and content.

strategiestargetsFactor.name: Multiple Representations: Number Line
strategiestargetsFactor.description: Easy access to seeing the relationships between numbers promotes Number Sense as students see these connections repeatedly.

strategiestargetsFactor.name: Music & Dance
strategiestargetsFactor.description: Connecting information to music and dance can support Short-term and Long-term Memory by engaging auditory processes, Emotions, and physical activity.

strategiestargetsFactor.name: Reciprocal Teaching
strategiestargetsFactor.description: Students deepen their understanding and gain confidence in their learning when they explain to and receive feedback from others.

strategiestargetsFactor.name: Student-generated Problems
strategiestargetsFactor.description: When students create their own number and word problems, they connect math concepts to their background knowledge and lived experiences.

strategiestargetsFactor.name: Videos
strategiestargetsFactor.description: Providing visuals to introduce, support, or review instruction activates more cognitive processes to support learning.

strategiestargetsFactor.name: Worked Examples
strategiestargetsFactor.description: Analyzing and discussing solved problems helps students develop a deeper understanding of abstract mathematical processes.

learnerModelshasFactor.name: Building Math 3-6
learnerModelshasFactor.description: The goals for students’ math skills in Grades 3-6 include thinking mathematically—that is, connecting mathematical concepts to each other and modeling the world with math. Understanding the Learner Factors and strategies that impact math skills and how they connect to each other can help you build tools and lessons that support all learners.

interactsWithFactorFactors.name: Hearing
interactsWithFactorFactors.description: We typically learn to understand many early math concepts through what we hear, but also what we can touch, see, and manipulate.

interactsWithFactorFactors.name: Physical Well-being
interactsWithFactorFactors.description: The benefits of physical health go beyond our bodies—our cognitive skills also improve with physical fitness.

interactsWithFactorFactors.name: Arithmetic Fact Retrieval
interactsWithFactorFactors.description: Arithmetic Fact Retrieval requires efficiently, accurately, and flexibly drawing basic number combinations from Long-term Memory to use in performing more complex calculations.

interactsWithFactorFactors.name: Algebraic Thinking
interactsWithFactorFactors.description: Algebraic Thinking is the ability to generalize, represent, justify, and reason with abstract mathematical structures and relationships.

interactsWithFactorFactors.name: Mathematical Flexibility
interactsWithFactorFactors.description: Mathematical Flexibility is the ability to maintain and shift among multiple representations of numbers and between problem-solving strategies in an adaptive manner.

interactsWithFactorFactors.name: Math Communication
interactsWithFactorFactors.description: Language and literacy skills support many aspects of math problem solving.

interactsWithFactorFactors.name: Proportional Reasoning
interactsWithFactorFactors.description: Proportional Reasoning involves an understanding of ratio and the relationships between ratios.

interactsWithFactorFactors.name: Number Sense
interactsWithFactorFactors.description: Number Sense includes both the conceptual understanding of whole and rational numbers and their magnitude, and the ability to represent and operate with these numbers.

interactsWithFactorFactors.name: Measurement
interactsWithFactorFactors.description: Measurement involves identifying an abstract spatial or temporal component of an entity (e.g., length) and comparing it to a measure unit that has the same attribute (e.g., an inch, a minute) so that the component can be assigned a numerical value, readily reasoned with, and used in calculation.

interactsWithFactorFactors.name: Emotion
interactsWithFactorFactors.description: Emotions are complex psychological states stemming from our positive and negative experiences.

interactsWithFactorFactors.name: Math Mindset
interactsWithFactorFactors.description: Math Mindset includes learners' self-concept and self-efficacy beliefs as well as their mindset toward failure, all of which shape their willingness to get involved with mathematics.

interactsWithFactorFactors.name: Stereotype Threat
interactsWithFactorFactors.description: In our society, there are many stereotypes that exist about the academic abilities of learners based on characteristics such as their race, gender, disability, and socioeconomic status.

interactsWithFactorFactors.name: Sensory Integration
interactsWithFactorFactors.description: We are constantly taking in information––particularly sights, smells, and sounds–– and our Sensory Integration skills help us make sense of it all.

interactsWithFactorFactors.name: Attention
interactsWithFactorFactors.description: Attention is the ability to focus on a specific task without being distracted.

interactsWithFactorFactors.name: Long-term Memory
interactsWithFactorFactors.description: Long-term Memory can store information indefinitely.

interactsWithFactorFactors.name: Metacognition
interactsWithFactorFactors.description: Metacognition refers to the ability to think about our own thinking and to pay attention to and control our cognitive processes.

interactsWithFactorFactors.name: Cognitive Flexibility
interactsWithFactorFactors.description: Cognitive Flexibility, a component of executive functioning, is the ability to effectively adapt our behavior as we face changing environmental and task demands.

interactsWithFactorFactors.name: Cognitive Flexibility
interactsWithFactorFactors.description: Cognitive Flexibility, a component of executive functioning, is the ability to effectively adapt our behavior as we face changing environmental and task demands.

interactsWithFactorFactors.name: Inhibition
interactsWithFactorFactors.description: Inhibition, a component of executive functioning, is the ability to suppress Attention to irrelevant input and to focus on pertinent stimuli or information.

interactsWithFactorFactors.name: Reasoning
interactsWithFactorFactors.description: Reasoning is the ability to think abstractly, draw inferences, identify patterns and relationships, and apply logic in order to flexibly solve novel problems.

interactsWithFactorFactors.name: Spatial Skills
interactsWithFactorFactors.description: We use our Spatial Skills to mentally manipulate objects and numbers.

interactsWithFactorFactors.name: Visual Processing
interactsWithFactorFactors.description: Visual Processing is seeing at the cognitive level: taking the input that comes through our Vision and working to understand what we see.

prerequisiteStandards.description: Understand division as an unknown-factor problem. *For example, find $32 \div 8$ by finding the number that makes 32 when multiplied by 8.*
Apply and extend previous understandings of division to divide unit fractions by whole numbers and whole numbers by unit fractions.

futureDependentStandards.description: Solve real-world and mathematical problems by writing and solving equations of the form $x + p = q$ and $px = q$ for cases in which $p$, $q$ and $x$ are all nonnegative rational numbers.
Apply properties of operations as strategies to multiply and divide rational numbers.

Informally assess the degree of visual overlap of two numerical data distributions with similar variabilities, measuring the difference between the centers by expressing it as a multiple of a measure of variability. *For example, the mean height of players on the basketball team is 10 cm greater than the mean height of players on the soccer team, about twice the variability (mean absolute deviation) on either team; on a dot plot, the separation between the two distributions of heights is noticeable.*
